grammar.title: Third conditional
grammar.explanation_pt:
O **third conditional** fala de situações **imaginárias no passado** — algo que **não aconteceu** e sua consequência também imaginária.

**Estrutura: If + past perfect, would have + particípio**
- "If I **had studied** harder, I **would have passed** the exam." (Não estudei → não passei)
- "If she **hadn't missed** the bus, they **wouldn't have met**." (Ela perdeu → eles se conheceram)

**Contrações na fala (muito importantes):**
- **I'd** = I had (na parte do if) / I would (na consequência): "If **I'd** known, **I'd** have called."
- **would have** → **would've** ("uúdav"); **wouldn't have** → **wouldn't've**

**Outros modais na consequência:**
- **could have + pp** = poderia ter (possibilidade/habilidade): "If we'd left earlier, we **could have caught** the train."
- **might have + pp** = talvez tivesse: "If you'd asked, she **might have said** yes."

**Perguntas:** "What **would** you **have done** if you **had lost** your passport?"

**A ordem pode inverter** (sem vírgula): "I would have helped **if** you'd asked me."

**Inversão formal (sem if):** "**Had I known**, I would have come." (= If I had known) — comum em textos formais e no B2 First.

⚠️ **Nunca** use "would have" na oração com if: ❌ "If I would have known..."

rows: I didn't study, so I failed.
If I had studied, I would have passed.
It rained, so we cancelled the trip.
If it hadn't rained, we wouldn't have cancelled the trip.
I didn't know, so I didn't help.
If I'd known, I could have helped.
She took the job in Lisbon and met her husband.
If she hadn't taken the job, she might not have met him.

examples.en: If I hadn't taken that English course, I would never have got this job.
examples.pt: Se eu não tivesse feito aquele curso de inglês, nunca teria conseguido este emprego.

examples.en: We could have avoided the problem if we'd checked the numbers.
examples.pt: Poderíamos ter evitado o problema se tivéssemos conferido os números.

examples.en: Had the firefighters arrived five minutes later, the whole building might have burned down.
examples.pt: Se os bombeiros tivessem chegado cinco minutos depois, o prédio todo poderia ter pegado fogo.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português, na fala, muitas vezes dizemos "se eu **soubesse**, eu **tinha** te contado" para o passado. Em inglês, use sempre a estrutura completa: **If I had known, I would have told you.**

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have come.
common_mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have come.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Na oração com if, use past perfect (had + pp).

common_mistakes.wrong: If I had studied, I would passed.
common_mistakes.right: If I had studied, I would have passed.

common_mistakes.wrong: If she didn't miss the bus, they wouldn't have met.
common_mistakes.right: If she hadn't missed the bus, they wouldn't have met.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Hipótese sobre o passado = past perfect.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Nativos quase nunca dizem "would have" por extenso: **would've** = "**uúdav**", **could've** = "**kúdav**", **wouldn't have** = "**uúdentav**". E "If I'd known, I'd have..." = "if áid nôun, áidav...". Treine o ouvido — e use na fala.

listening.context_pt: Um homem conta num podcast como escapou de um acidente por pouco.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.en: It was a Monday, and I was running late for work, which almost never happens. I was so annoyed — I'd forgotten to set my alarm. When I finally got to the bus stop, the bus had just left. I remember thinking, "If I'd woken up five minutes earlier, I would have caught it." About ten minutes later, I heard sirens. That bus had been involved in a serious accident on the highway. Several passengers were injured. If I'd been on time that day, I would have been sitting in my usual seat — right at the front, where the impact happened. I'm not a superstitious person, but since then, I've never complained about being late.

reading.title: History's great "what ifs"
reading.text: Historians are often cautious about "counterfactual" questions — imagining what would have happened if events had been different — but these questions can help us understand how fragile history really is. Consider the discovery of penicillin. In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mould had contaminated one of his bacterial cultures — and that the bacteria around the mould had died. If he had cleaned his laboratory before leaving, or if the mould had landed on a different plate, he might never have noticed the effect. Penicillin, and the antibiotics that followed, have since saved millions of lives. Or take the Post-it note, which we saw in an earlier unit: if Spencer Silver hadn't "failed" to make a strong glue, one of the world's most famous office products would not have been invented. Of course, history is rarely shaped by a single moment. Had Fleming not noticed the mould, someone else might eventually have discovered penicillin. Still, these stories remind us that chance, curiosity and the ability to notice the unexpected have played a much larger role in human progress than we usually admit.

questions.q: What might have happened if he'd cleaned his lab before leaving?

questions.q: What do these stories remind us?

writing.model:
The email I almost didn't send

In 2019, I was working as an accountant in a job I didn't enjoy. One evening, I saw an online advert for a course in graphic design. The deadline for applications was midnight, and it was already eleven o'clock. I was tired, and I almost closed the laptop.

If I had gone to bed that night, my life would have been completely different. I would probably still be working in accounting, and I might never have discovered how much I love design. I wouldn't have met Lucas, my teacher on the course, who later offered me my first freelance project. And if he hadn't recommended me to his clients, I couldn't have built my own studio, which now has four employees.

Of course, things could have gone wrong. If the course had been terrible, I might have lost money and confidence. Had my family not supported me, I would never have had the courage to quit my stable job.

With hindsight, I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I'd made the change earlier. But I don't really regret the years in accounting: they taught me how to manage a business. Sometimes, the turning point isn't a big event. It's an email you send at 11:57 p.m.

grammar.title: Mixed conditionals
grammar.explanation_pt:
Os condicionais "puros" mantêm o mesmo tempo nas duas partes. Mas a vida real mistura tempos! Os **mixed conditionals** combinam partes do **second** e do **third** conditional.

**Tipo 1: condição no PASSADO → resultado no PRESENTE**
**If + past perfect, would + verbo base (now)**
- "If I **had accepted** the job in Canada, I **would be living** there **now**." (não aceitei → não moro lá hoje)
- "If she **hadn't studied** medicine, she **wouldn't be** a doctor today."
- "If we **had saved** more, we **wouldn't have** these money problems **now**."

**Tipo 2: característica PRESENTE (permanente) → resultado no PASSADO**
**If + past simple, would have + particípio**
- "If I **were** more confident, I **would have spoken** in the meeting yesterday." (não sou confiante → não falei)
- "If he **didn't have** a fear of flying, he **would have come** to the wedding."
- "If I **spoke** French, I **would have understood** the film."

**Como escolher?** Pergunte-se: **quando** é a condição? **Quando** é o resultado?
- passado → passado = **third** (If I'd known, I'd have come)
- presente/geral → presente/futuro = **second** (If I knew, I'd come)
- passado → presente = **mixed tipo 1** (If I'd known, I'd be there now)
- presente → passado = **mixed tipo 2** (If I knew him, I'd have invited him)

**Palavras-pista:** now, today, still (presente) / yesterday, last year, in 2015 (passado).

rows: If I had money, I'd travel.
If I'd had money, I'd have travelled.
If I'd saved money, I'd be travelling now.

grammar.tip_pt: Mixed conditionals são muito comuns na **fala natural** — muitas vezes até mais que os puros. Ouvir "If I'd known, I wouldn't be here" num filme é muito frequente!

reading.title: The road not taken
reading.text: "Two roads diverged in a wood, and I — / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." These lines from Robert Frost's 1916 poem "The Road Not Taken" are among the most quoted in American literature, often printed on posters encouraging people to be brave and different. Yet many literary critics argue that the poem is widely misunderstood. Earlier in the poem, Frost actually describes the two roads as being worn "really about the same". The traveller only imagines that, years later, he will tell the story as if his choice had been dramatic and meaningful. In other words, the poem may be less about bravery and more about how we construct stories about our decisions after the fact. Psychologists have found something similar: we tend to justify our choices once they are made, convincing ourselves that the path we took was the right one. If we had chosen differently, we would probably be just as good at explaining why that choice was the best. Perhaps that's not a bad thing. If we didn't have this ability, we might spend our lives tormented by the roads we didn't take.

questions.q: How are Frost's lines usually interpreted?
questions.answer: As encouraging people to be brave and different.

questions.q: Why do critics say the poem is misunderstood?
questions.answer: Frost describes the two roads as being about the same; the traveller only imagines telling it as dramatic later.

questions.q: What have psychologists found about our choices?
questions.answer: We tend to justify them once they're made.

questions.q: Why might this ability be a good thing?
questions.answer: Without it, we might be tormented by the roads we didn't take.

writing.model:
Is it better to regret what you did, or what you didn't do?

A famous saying claims that we regret the things we didn't do more than the things we did. Research by psychologists has offered some support for this idea: in the short term, people tend to regret their mistakes, but over a lifetime, they regret their missed opportunities more.

My own experience supports this view. When I was 22, I was offered a scholarship to study in Germany, but I turned it down because I was afraid of leaving my family. If I had accepted it, I would probably speak German fluently now, and I might be working in a completely different field. If I weren't so attached to my home, I would have taken that chance without hesitation. Even today, I sometimes wonder what might have been.

On the other hand, my brother took a risk that went wrong. He invested in a restaurant that closed after a year. If he hadn't opened it, he would have saved a lot of money. Yet he insists he has no regrets. If he hadn't tried, he says, he would still be dreaming about it today instead of having learned so much about business. Had he not failed, he wouldn't have started the successful catering company he runs now.

In my opinion, regrets about actions usually teach us something, while regrets about inaction stay with us as unanswered questions. Therefore, I believe it is generally better to take reasonable risks than to play it safe forever.

grammar.title: Wish, if only, it's time, would rather
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Wish / If only + past simple** → desejo sobre o **presente** (revisão):
"I **wish** I **had** more free time." / "**If only** I **were** taller!"

**2. Wish / If only + past perfect** → arrependimento sobre o **passado**:
- "I **wish** I **had studied** harder at school." (não estudei — me arrependo)
- "**If only** I **hadn't said** that!"
- "She **wishes** she **had taken** the job in London."

**3. Wish + would / wouldn't** → **reclamação** sobre o comportamento de **outra pessoa** ou situação que queremos que mude:
- "I **wish** you **would** stop leaving your clothes on the floor!"
- "I **wish** it **would** stop raining."
⚠️ Não use "I wish I would..." (sobre você mesmo, use could: "I wish I **could** stop procrastinating").

**4. It's (high / about) time + sujeito + past simple** → já passou da hora de algo acontecer (crítica/urgência):
- "**It's time** we **went** home." / "**It's high time** the government **did** something about it."
- Também: **It's time to** + verbo (mais neutro): "It's time to go."

**5. Would rather + sujeito + past simple** → preferência sobre o que **outra pessoa** faz:
- "**I'd rather you didn't** smoke here." (prefiro que você não fume — educado!)
- "**I'd rather** we **met** tomorrow."
- Compare com **I'd rather + verbo base** (sobre você mesmo): "I'd rather stay home."

**Resumo do "backshift" para irrealidade:** presente → past simple · passado → past perfect.

I wish I hadn't bought that car.
I wish he would call me.
It's time you got a job.

listening.title: The top five regrets
listening.context_pt: Uma apresentadora fala sobre o livro de uma enfermeira de cuidados paliativos.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Australian palliative care nurse Bronnie Ware spent years caring for people in the last weeks of their lives, and she wrote about the regrets they shared with her. Her list became famous around the world. Many of her patients said: "I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself, not the life others expected of me." Others said: "I wish I hadn't worked so hard." Some told her: "I wish I'd had the courage to express my feelings," and "I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends." And finally: "I wish I had let myself be happier." What's striking is that none of these regrets is about money or possessions. They're all about courage, relationships and choices — things we can still change today.

reading.title: Learning from regret
reading.text: Regret has a bad reputation. We're often told to "live with no regrets" and to avoid dwelling on the past. But some psychologists argue that regret, when handled well, is one of our most useful emotions. In his book The Power of Regret, Daniel Pink describes a large survey in which thousands of people around the world shared their regrets. He identified four core types: foundation regrets ("If only I'd saved more money / looked after my health"), boldness regrets ("I wish I'd asked her out / started that business"), moral regrets ("I wish I hadn't cheated / been unkind") and connection regrets ("I wish I had kept in touch with my brother"). Interestingly, regrets about inaction — the chances we didn't take — tend to last longer than regrets about actions. Pink suggests a three-step method for using regret productively. First, reframe it: talk about it or write it down, which reduces its emotional power. Second, be kind to yourself — treat your past self as you would treat a friend who made a mistake. Third, extract a lesson for the future: "Next time, I'll speak up." Regret, in this view, isn't something to avoid. It's information about what we value most.

questions.q: What are the four core types of regret Pink identified?
questions.answer: Foundation, boldness, moral and connection regrets.

questions.q: Which regrets tend to last longer?
questions.answer: Regrets about inaction (chances not taken).

questions.q: What is the first step of Pink's method?
questions.answer: Reframe it: talk about it or write it down.

questions.q: What does regret tell us, according to this view?
questions.answer: What we value most.

writing.model:
Dear 17-year-old me,

I know you won't listen to everything I'm about to say — I certainly wouldn't have — but I'll try anyway.

First, I wish you had taken English more seriously at school. You thought you'd never need it. If only you'd known that, fifteen years later, you would be using it in meetings every day! You'll learn it eventually, but the hard way, in evening classes after long days at work.

Secondly, I wish you hadn't worried so much about what other people thought. You spent so much energy trying to fit in. I'd rather you spent that energy on the things you actually love: drawing, music, the friends who accept you exactly as you are.

I also wish you had told Grandpa how much he meant to you. He knew, I think — but I wish you'd said it out loud.

Here's the good news: you turn out fine. Better than fine, actually. You find work you enjoy, and people who love you.

So, it's high time you stopped waiting for the "perfect moment" to start things. It doesn't exist. Sign up for the art course. Call your friends. Say "I love you" more often.

And please — start using sunscreen.

With love,
Your older (and slightly wiser) self

grammar.title: Alternatives to if
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Suppose / Supposing / Imagine / What if** → introduzem **cenários hipotéticos** (no lugar de if). Funcionam com qualquer tipo de condicional:
- "**Suppose** you **won** the lottery — what **would** you do?" (second)
- "**Supposing** the flight **is** cancelled, what **will** we do?" (first)
- "**What if** we **had** missed the train?" (third)

**2. Otherwise / Or else** → "se não" — mostram a **consequência negativa** se algo não acontecer:
- "Save your work, **otherwise** you'll lose it." (= If you don't save it, you'll lose it.)
- "Leave now, **or else** you'll miss the bus."
- Também no passado: "I took a taxi; **otherwise** I would have been late."

**3. But for + substantivo** (formal) = "não fosse por" (if it weren't for / if it hadn't been for):
- "**But for** the rain, the festival would have been perfect."
- "**If it hadn't been for** your help, I would have failed."
- "**If it weren't for** my family, I wouldn't be here."

**4. In case** → **precaução** (fazer algo agora por causa de uma possibilidade futura):
- "Take an umbrella **in case** it rains." (leve agora — talvez chova)
- Compare: "Take an umbrella **if** it rains." (só leve se estiver chovendo)
- **In case of** + substantivo (avisos): "**In case of** fire, use the stairs."

**5. Even if** → mesmo que (a condição não muda o resultado): "**Even if** it rains, we'll go."

**6. Revisão B1+/B2:** **unless** (a menos que), **provided / providing (that)**, **as long as**, **on condition that**.

listening.title: Emergency preparedness
listening.context_pt: Um especialista da Defesa Civil fala sobre como se preparar para emergências.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.en: Suppose a major storm hit your city tonight and you lost electricity and water for three days. Would you be ready? Most people wouldn't. Here's what I recommend. Keep at least three days of water and non-perishable food at home, in case of emergencies. Have a power bank fully charged, otherwise you could lose all communication. Keep copies of important documents in a waterproof bag or in the cloud. And agree on a meeting point with your family, in case you can't reach each other by phone. Even if you think it'll never happen to you, it takes only a few hours to prepare. In my experience, but for these simple steps, many families would have suffered much more during recent floods.

questions.q: What scenario does the expert ask us to imagine?
questions.answer: A major storm with no electricity and water for three days.

questions.q: How much water and food should you keep?
questions.answer: At least three days' worth (non-perishable food).

questions.q: Why should you have a charged power bank?
questions.answer: Otherwise you could lose all communication.

questions.q: Why should families agree on a meeting point?
questions.answer: In case they can't reach each other by phone.

reading.title: Thinking in scenarios
reading.text: In the early 1970s, the oil company Shell began using a technique called scenario planning. Instead of trying to predict a single future, its planners imagined several possible futures and asked: "Suppose this happened — how would we respond?" One of the scenarios they explored was a sudden, dramatic rise in oil prices. Most companies considered this unlikely. When the oil crisis of 1973 arrived, Shell was widely seen as being better prepared than many of its competitors, and the company's approach became famous in business schools. Today, scenario planning is used by governments, cities and businesses around the world. The idea is not to guess correctly, but to become more flexible. A city might ask: "What if sea levels rose faster than expected?" or "Supposing a pandemic closed schools for months, how would children learn?" The process often reveals weaknesses that nobody had noticed. Psychologists point out that individuals can benefit from the same thinking. Imagining a worst-case scenario — and planning how you would cope — can actually reduce anxiety, because the future feels less threatening once you have a plan. As the old saying goes: hope for the best, but prepare for the worst.

questions.q: What is scenario planning?
questions.answer: Imagining several possible futures and planning responses, instead of predicting one.

questions.q: What scenario helped Shell before 1973?
questions.answer: A sudden, dramatic rise in oil prices.

questions.q: What is the main goal of scenario planning?
questions.answer: To become more flexible, not to guess correctly.

questions.q: How can it help individuals?
questions.answer: Imagining a worst case and planning for it can reduce anxiety.

writing.task: Write a practical guide (200–250 words) titled "What if...? Be prepared!" for one situation (a trip abroad, a job interview, a natural disaster, a wedding). Use at least 7 alternatives to if.
writing.task_pt: Escreva um guia prático (200–250 palavras) intitulado "What if...? Be prepared!" para uma situação (viagem ao exterior, entrevista de emprego, desastre natural, casamento). Use pelo menos 7 alternativas ao if.
writing.model:
What if...? Be prepared for your first trip abroad!

Travelling abroad for the first time is exciting, but things don't always go as planned. Here's how to be ready for the most common problems.

Supposing you lose your passport, what would you do? Before you leave, take a photo of it and save a copy in the cloud, in case you need to prove your identity at the embassy. Also, write down your country's embassy phone number — your phone might be stolen too!

What if your bank card stops working? Always carry two different cards and some cash, otherwise you could be stuck without money on your first night. Tell your bank you're travelling, or else your card might be blocked for "suspicious activity".

Travel insurance is essential. Even if you're young and healthy, a hospital bill abroad can be extremely expensive. Many travellers have told me that, but for their insurance, an accident would have ruined them financially.

Finally, plan your first day carefully. Book your first night's accommodation in advance, as long as you can cancel it for free, and know how to get there from the airport.

Of course, you can't predict everything. But if you prepare for the worst-case scenario, you'll be able to relax and enjoy the best parts of your adventure. Bon voyage!

culture_note.title: "Hope for the best, prepare for the worst"
culture_note.text_pt: Culturas variam muito na forma de lidar com incerteza. O pesquisador Geert Hofstede chamou isso de **uncertainty avoidance**: países como Alemanha e Japão tendem a planejar tudo; outros, como o Brasil, costumam ser mais flexíveis e improvisar — o famoso **"jeitinho"**. Em equipes internacionais, combinar planejamento e flexibilidade é uma grande vantagem.

summary_pt: Suppose / supposing / what if = cenários hipotéticos.
but for / if it hadn't been for = não fosse por.
in case = por precaução (≠ if) · even if = mesmo que.
